Re-analysing ADVANCE with the Win Ratio

Severine Bompoint

2026-09-07

WINS examples

Example 1: a binary outcome

There is an example dataset called data_binary included in WINS for demonstration:

library(WINS)


head(data_binary)
##   id arm Y_1 Y_2 Y_3
## 1  1   A   0   0   0
## 2  2   A   0   0   1
## 3  3   A   1   1   0
## 4  4   A   1   1   0
## 5  5   A   1   1   1
## 6  6   A   0   0   0

We have columns:

  • id, identifying patients
  • arm, identifying treatment arm
  • and binary outcomes Y_1, Y_2, and Y_3.

We can calculate a win-ratio using hierarchy \(Y_1 > Y_2 > Y_3\):

win.stat(
  data = data_binary,
  ep_type = c("binary"),
  arm.name = c("A","B"),
  priority = c(1, 2, 3),
  stratum.weight = "unstratified",
  pvalue = "two-sided",
  summary.print = TRUE
)
## The outcome type for all the endpoints:  binary 
## This analysis is unstratified. 
## 
##  Win Ratio : 2.29854 
##  
##  two-sided p-value is:  0.00010 
##  Lower limit of 95 % CI of the win ratio:  1.51060 
##  Upper limit of 95 % CI of the win ratio:  3.49746 
##  
##  
##  Net Benefit : 0.27780 
##  
##  two-sided p-value is:  0.00024 
##  Lower limit of 95 % CI of the net benefit:  0.12969 
##  Upper limit of 95 % CI of the net benefit:  0.42591 
##  
##  
##  Win Odds : 1.76932 
##  
##  two-sided p-value is:  0.00016 
##  Lower limit of 95 % CI of the win odds:  1.31571 
##  Upper limit of 95 % CI of the win odds:  2.37930 
## 
## NULL

The function win.stat assumes it will find outcome columns named Y_1, Y_2, etc in data_binary. The parameter priority = c(1, 2, 3) tells it to resolve wins by first looking at Y_1, followed by Y_2, and then finally Y_3. If we added a forth outcome with lowest priority, we would name it Y_4 and specify priority = c(1, 2, 3, 4).

Note ep_type = c("binary"), telling the function that all of our outcomes are binary. See https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/WINS/vignettes/vignette.pdf for examples with a mixture of outcome types.

Amongst R functions, win.stat in WINS is somewhat unusual in that by default it prints analysis to the console. If you want to assign the analysis object to a variable name, like wins_all, you need to include the parameter summary.print = FALSE:

wins_all <- win.stat(
  data = data_binary,
  ep_type = c("binary"),
  arm.name = c("A","B"),
  priority = c(1, 2, 3),
  stratum.weight = "unstratified",
  pvalue = "two-sided",
  summary.print = FALSE
)
## The outcome type for all the endpoints:  binary 
## This analysis is unstratified.

wins-all is now an object in the R session:

print(wins_all)
## $Win_prop
##   stratum     P_trt     P_con
## 1       1 0.4917333 0.2139333
## 
## $Win_statistic
## $Win_statistic$Win_Ratio
##       WR     WR_L     WR_U 
## 2.298535 1.510603 3.497455 
## 
## $Win_statistic$Net_Benefit
##        NB      NB_L      NB_U 
## 0.2778000 0.1296935 0.4259065 
## 
## $Win_statistic$Win_Odds
##       WO     WO_L     WO_U 
## 1.769316 1.315715 2.379299 
## 
## 
## $z_statistic

Individual elements can be plucked out:

wins_all$Win_statistic$Win_Ratio[1]
##       WR 
## 2.298535

Example 2: a continuous outcome (cont.)

Likewise, there is a test dataset in WINS that contains continuous outcomes:

head(data_continuous)
##   id arm       Y_1       Y_2         Y_3
## 1  1   A 0.4621177 0.2069386 -0.52627613
## 2  2   A 0.3258938 0.2595162 -0.11247766
## 3  3   A 2.4887816 0.5406375 -0.34632514
## 4  4   A 3.9419121 0.4956837 -0.44683113
## 5  5   A 2.3304126 0.5481473 -0.02682927
## 6  6   A 0.3168587 0.1186624 -1.85656323
win.stat(
  data = data_continuous,
  ep_type = c("continuous"),
  arm.name = c("A","B"),
  priority = c(1, 2, 3),
  stratum.weight = "unstratified",
  pvalue = "two-sided",
  summary.print = TRUE
)
## The outcome type for all the endpoints:  continuous 
## This analysis is unstratified. 
## 
##  Win Ratio : 1.69542 
##

##

Note ep_type = c("continuous"), telling the function that all of our outcomes are continuous.

Example 3: a time-to-event outcome (cont.)

There is also a test dataset in WINS that contains time-to-event outcomes:

head(data_tte)
##   id arm Delta_1 Delta_2 Delta_3       Y_1       Y_2       Y_3
## 1  1   A       0       0       0 0.1268054 2.9063267 0.2605294
## 2  2   A       0       1       1 1.0137019 1.7945845 1.5220050
## 3  3   A       1       0       0 1.4323415 1.5009229 0.6054241
## 4  4   A       1       1       0 1.6961593 5.1323268 1.9331923
## 5  5   A       1       0       1 3.5786849 0.4329275 0.6391820
## 6  6   A       1       1       0 0.5615477 8.2259638 0.5401791

In contrast to the binary and continuous outcomes, the time-to-event outcomes require two columns each: Y_1 (e.g.) containing the event time, possibly censored; and Delta_1 (e.g.) containing a binary indicator of whether the event occurred (i.e. 1) or was censored (0).

win.stat(
  data = data_tte,
  ep_type = c("tte"),
  arm.name = c("A","B"),
  priority = c(1, 2, 3),
  stratum.weight = "unstratified",
  pvalue = "two-sided",
  summary.print = TRUE
)
## The outcome type for all the endpoints:  tte 
## This analysis is unstratified. 
## 
##  Win Ratio : 2.19636 
##  
##  two-sided p-value is:  < 1e-05 
##  Lower limit of 95 % CI of the win ratio:  1.71633 
##  Upper limit of 95 % CI of the win ratio:  2.81064 
##  
##  
##  Net Benefit : 0.33663 
##  
##  two-sided p-value is:  < 1e-05 
##  Lower limit of 95 % CI of the net benefit:  0.22573 
##  Upper limit of 95 % CI of the net benefit:  0.44752 
##  
##  
##  Win Odds : 2.01489 
##  
##  two-sided p-value is:  < 1e-05 
##  Lower limit of 95 % CI of the win odds:  1.61408 
##  Upper limit of 95 % CI of the win odds:  2.51522 
## 
## NULL

Note ep_type = c("tte"), telling the function that all of our outcomes are time-to-event.

Example 4: Plotting the win proportion for tte endpoints over the study time

This is a simulated example with two TTE endpoints.

data <- sim.data(
  n_trt = 200,
  n_con = 200,
  n_ep = 2,
  arm.name = c("A","B"),
  ep_type = "tte",
  cdist.rate = 0.5,
  sim_method = "copula",
  copula_trt=copula::normalCopula(0.9),
  margins_trt=c("gamma", "beta"),
  paramMargins_trt=list(list(shape=2, scale=1),
                        list(shape1=2, shape2=2)),
  copula_con=copula::normalCopula(0.9),
  margins_con=c("gamma", "beta"),
  paramMargins_con=list(list(shape=2, scale=1),
                        list(shape1=2, shape2=2)),
  max_accrual_time = 5
)
## [1] "The outcome type for all the endpoints: tte"
partition_t.plot(
  data, 
  Ctime = seq(0,8,0.2), 
  arm.name = c("A","B"), 
  priority = c(1,2), 
  tau = 0, 
  plotTimeUnit = "days", 
  trt_group = "both"
)

Example 5: Plotting the Win Statistics for tte endpoints over the study time

This is a simulated example with two TTE endpoints.

stat_t.plot(
  data, 
  arm.name = c("A","B"),
  priority = c(1,2), 
  Ctime = seq(2,12,1),
  plotTimeUnit = "years",
  statistic = "WR", 
  tau = 0, 
  stratum.weight = "unstratified", 
  plot_CI = TRUE
)

George Institute Cumulative analysis

In the re-analysis of the ADVANCE trial and in other George Institute trials, we have produced cumulative analyses to examine the relative impact of the outcome hierarchy in the overall win ratio estimate. By cumulative analyses, for a given outcome hierarchy we mean examining the win ratio based only on the first component, then on the first two components, and so on until all components are used (i.e. using the full hierarchy). This entailed writing some functions that would perform the incremental analysis and created the notion of a data-package, comprising a dataset to send to WINS, plus the label, type, and min difference (tau) for each variable.

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

data_package <- list( 
  # Example dataset provided by WINS package 
  df = data_binary %>% 
    mutate( 
      # In our functions, arm column must contain T and C, so recode: 
      arm = case_when( 
        arm == "A" ~ "T", 
        arm == "B" ~ "C", 
        .default = NA 
      )
    ), 
  ep_type = c("binary", "binary", "binary"), 
  tau = c(0, 0, 0), 
  labels = c("Mortality", "+ Hospitalisation", "+ AE") # For example 
)

# Cumulative analysis:
source("functions.R")
x <- 
  run_cumulative_analysis(
    data_package = data_package,
    priority = c(1, 2, 3)
  )
## The outcome type for all the endpoints:  binary 
## This analysis is unstratified. 
## This analysis is unstratified. 
## This analysis is unstratified.

Example 6 - the decision tree

wr_cumulative_flow_plot(x,
  plot_title = "My trial"
)

Example 7 - cumulative plot

wr_cumulative_panel_plot(x)
